The [Decision Models](/reference/lookups/decision-models/) lookup ends on a claim this lab exists to
test: a decision model's probability is only worth acting on if it is calibrated, and nobody has
measured that independently. This lab measures it, for the one decision model whose weights are
open — **Laya**, Apache-2.0 — on **human-labelled** data, zero-shot: the version a team gets on its
first day.

Source: [`labs/decision-tier-calibration`](https://github.com/vins13pattar/principal-ai-engineer-handbook/tree/main/labs/decision-tier-calibration)

<Aside type="caution" title="production-shaped, and what that means here">
  The model, the data, and the measurements are real: `laya==0.4.1` at a pinned revision, 1,000
  rows per set, run on Apple silicon. What is held fixed is the setting — zero-shot, no fine-tuning,
  one phrasing per question unless stated. Laya's own card says fine-tuning drives its headline
  accuracy, so these numbers describe the out-of-the-box model, not its ceiling. The measurement runs
  locally; CI re-derives every number below from the committed results without the model.
</Aside>

## Why not the benchmark everyone cites

TypeSafe's eval suite — the one Laya, Jev, and Clef all report against — labels its cases by a
consensus of OpenAI and Anthropic models. Its own card says so: the labels are model-generated
references. An accuracy figure on it measures agreement with LLMs, and calibration against it would
be calibration to LLM agreement. It also declares no license.

So this lab uses three sets labelled by people, under explicit licenses:
`zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment` (MIT), `fancyzhx/amazon_polarity` (Apache-2.0), and
Banking77 (CC-BY-4.0). Only numbers are committed — the row index, the human label, and the
probabilities — never the text.

## Finding 1: one rewording, from chance to 91%

The same 1,000 Amazon reviews, the same decision, asked three ways:

| Question | Accuracy | ECE as shipped |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `noul`: "Is this product review positive?" | **52.9%** — the majority baseline | 0.477 |
| `noul`: "Does the reviewer like the product?" | 91.2% | 0.076 |
| `choice`: negative / positive | 94.2% | 0.016 |

The first phrasing is not merely inaccurate. It is wrong with total confidence: **998 of 1,000
answers were stated at 100%**, and its probability of "yes" was effectively zero for positive and
negative reviews alike. A decision tier built on it would wave everything through, certain of
itself, and no threshold could catch it — there is nothing below the threshold to escalate.

This was found by accident. The first run asked only the first phrasing and scored chance; probing
whether the lab had misused the API turned up the second phrasing scoring 0.72 on a review the first
called 0.0000. Laya's card mentions that `noul` answers can follow their option labels rather than
the state. This is that, measured, and it means **a question's wording is part of the model's
configuration** — something to test, version, and regression-check like any other.

## Finding 2: at 77 options, confidence runs backwards

On Banking77, stated confidence against how often it was right:

| Stated confidence | Answers | Stated | Right |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.0 – 0.2 | 361 | 9.3% | 23.0% |
| 0.2 – 0.4 | 158 | 29.3% | 37.3% |
| 0.4 – 0.6 | 114 | 49.4% | 39.5% |
| 0.6 – 0.8 | 89 | 70.1% | 46.1% |
| 0.8 – 1.0 | 278 | 95.9% | **64.0%** |

Underconfident where it is unsure, badly overconfident where it is sure. A single temperature pushes
every answer the same way, so it cannot correct miscalibration that runs in both directions: fitting
one moved ECE from 0.178 to 0.177. And **no threshold reaches a 10% error rate** — answers given
0.99 or more were right 73% of the time. At this option count the probability is not a usable
escalation signal at all.

## Finding 3: at 3 options, it works

Financial-tweet sentiment is the case a decision tier is sold on, and it holds up. Calibration as
shipped is reasonable (ECE 0.059, slightly underconfident in the middle), and the operational test
passes: a threshold **fitted on one half for a 10% error rate delivered 11.0% on the other half**,
while keeping 61% of traffic. Two-option sentiment as a `choice` did better still — ECE 0.016, 6.3%
error on the held-out half with nothing escalated.

## Finding 4: temperature scaling is not a general fix

It improved ECE in two of five cases. One is real: the reworded `noul`, 0.076 to 0.026. The other
is not — on the broken phrasing it moved ECE from 0.477 to 0.262 only by teaching a coin flip to
admit it is one, with accuracy unchanged at 52.9%. On the other three it was neutral or slightly
worse. Minimising log-likelihood is not the same objective as making the top answer's confidence
honest, and the lab's numbers show the gap.

## What makes the numbers trustworthy

- **Every fit is judged on data it did not see.** Temperatures and thresholds are fitted on one
  seeded half and evaluated on the other.
- **The metric is cross-checked.** The lab's ECE was compared with Laya's own `ece_score` on all
  five measured sets and matches to four decimals.
- **The tests could fail.** Metric tests use synthetic records with miscalibration put there on
  purpose, and assert the metrics recover it — including that a threshold fitted on calibrated
  records misses its target on overconfident ones.
- **The report reproduces.** CI re-derives every figure on this page from the committed results,
  with no model, no network, and no GPU.

## Run it

```bash
cd labs/decision-tier-calibration
uv venv && uv pip install -e '.[dev]'
.venv/bin/python -m decision_tier report     # every number above, from committed results

uv pip install -e '.[measure]'               # local only: torch, laya, ~800 MB checkpoint
.venv/bin/python -m decision_tier measure    # re-measures and rewrites results/
```

## Principal-level discussion points

- **Is a decision tier worth it here?** Not a vendor question — a curve. Plot coverage against
  error on your own labelled traffic, and find the point you can live with. On three-way sentiment
  there is one; on 77-way intent there is not.
- **Who owns the wording?** If one phrasing scores chance and another 91%, the prompt is
  configuration with production consequences. It needs an owner, tests, and a review before it
  changes.
- **What is the threshold fitted on?** A threshold is a function of a model, a phrasing, and a
  traffic mix. Change any of them — including switching to an API-compatible competitor — and the
  threshold has to be fitted again.
